title: SSDs & Modern Storage I/O
summary: How flash storage breaks every HDD-era assumption — erase-before-write, write amplification, wear leveling, and why TRIM exists — closing out the group with the storage hardware everything above actually runs on today.

slides.markdown:
Every mental model built around HDDs — seek time, disk scheduling, rotational latency — assumes a physical arm and spinning platters. SSDs have neither. They introduce a completely different set of constraints: you can't overwrite flash in place, writes can silently balloon in size (write amplification), and cells wear out after a bounded number of erases.

This topic closes the I/O group with the storage medium underneath nearly everything built today — understanding *why* SSDs behave the way they do, not just that they're "fast," is what separates a surface-level answer from a staff-level one in any storage-adjacent interview.

An SSD stores data as electrical charge trapped in **floating-gate transistors**, organized into **pages** (typically 4-16KB, the smallest unit you can read or write) grouped into **blocks** (typically 128-256 pages, roughly 1-4MB, the smallest unit you can *erase*). There's no arm, no platter, no rotation — any page is electrically accessible in roughly the same small constant time, which is exactly why disk-scheduling algorithms built around seek distance ([Disk Scheduling Algorithms](disk-scheduling-algorithms)) don't apply here.

The asymmetry that drives everything else in this topic: you can *read* or *write* at page granularity, but you can only *erase* at the much larger block granularity — and a page must be erased before it can be written again.

slides.sectionTitle: Why you can't overwrite a flash page in place
slides.markdown:
Flash memory's physics only let a program operation move a cell's charge in one direction — writing a page can only flip bits from a fully-erased state (all 1s) toward the target pattern, never the reverse. To store new data in a page that's already written, the underlying cells must first be reset to their erased state, which — because erase only operates on whole blocks — means erasing every other still-valid page in that block too.

So the SSD controller can't simply "overwrite" your file's data the way an HDD does: it must find a free page elsewhere (or trigger an erase-and-rewrite cycle for the affected block), which is the root cause of both write amplification and the need for wear leveling, covered next.

slides.sectionTitle: Write amplification: a small write causing a much larger internal write
slides.markdown:
**Write amplification** is the ratio between the data an application actually asked to write and the data the SSD physically writes internally to accomplish it. Modifying a single 4KB page inside a block that still has other valid pages often forces the controller to read the entire block (say, 256KB), merge in the changed page, erase the whole block, and rewrite all 256KB — a single 4KB logical write triggering a 256KB physical write, a 64x amplification factor in the worst case.

This matters for two concrete reasons: it reduces effective write throughput under sustained random writes (the SSD is doing far more physical work than the logical request implies), and it accelerates wear, since every amplified byte written counts against the flash cell's limited erase-cycle lifespan.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: SSD block/page layout and the erase cycle
slides.markdown:
![SSD garbage collection reclaiming a block](assets/ssd-garbage-collection.svg)

The crossed-out pages represent data that's been logically overwritten or deleted but whose old physical location can't be reused until the entire block is erased — those pages sit there as dead weight until garbage collection reclaims the whole block.

This is the physical process underlying write amplification: relocating still-valid pages before erasing is real, extra I/O the application never asked for, done purely because of the erase-at-block-granularity constraint.

slides.sectionTitle: Wear leveling: spreading writes to avoid wearing out one region
slides.markdown:
Each flash block can survive only a bounded number of erase cycles before it becomes unreliable — commonly a few thousand for consumer TLC/QLC flash, tens of thousands for enterprise-grade SLC/MLC. If the same logical address were always mapped to the same physical block, a hot, frequently-updated region (a file system's journal, a database's write-ahead log) would wear out that one physical block long before the rest of the drive.

**Wear leveling** is the controller's strategy of spreading physical erase cycles evenly across the whole flash chip, regardless of which logical addresses are hottest — achieved via the same indirection layer (the Flash Translation Layer, or FTL) that maps logical block addresses to physical locations and can freely remap a logical address to a fresh, less-worn physical block on each rewrite.

slides.sectionTitle: The TRIM command: telling the SSD which blocks are actually free
slides.markdown:
When a file system deletes a file, it just updates its own metadata (marks blocks free in its bitmap) — it never tells the underlying storage device those physical blocks are no longer needed, because that concept doesn't exist for HDDs (an HDD just overwrites whatever's there, no matter what "used to be" in that spot). An SSD has no way to know a logical block is now garbage rather than genuinely stale-but-still-wanted data, so its garbage collector may keep relocating and preserving that dead data during background reclamation, wasting real write cycles.

The **TRIM** command (Linux: `fstrim`, or automatic via the `discard` mount option) closes this gap: the OS explicitly tells the SSD "these logical blocks are no longer in use," letting the controller's garbage collector skip preserving them entirely and erase them more efficiently — directly reducing write amplification and improving sustained write performance.

slides.sectionTitle: Garbage collection inside an SSD's controller
slides.markdown:
The SSD controller runs its own background **garbage collector**: it picks blocks with a favorable ratio of stale-to-valid pages, copies out the still-valid pages to a fresh location, erases the reclaimed block, and returns it to the free-block pool — all internal to the drive, invisible to the OS except through its effect on performance.

This background work competes with foreground application writes for the SSD's internal bandwidth, which is exactly why a drive that's been heavily used without TRIM (garbage collection preserving data it doesn't need to) can show noticeably degraded write throughput compared to a freshly formatted one — a very real, measurable performance regression, not a myth.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: HDD scheduling assumptions vs SSD reality
slides.markdown:
| | HDD | SSD |
|---|---|---|
| Access cost by location | Varies hugely — seek distance dominates | Roughly uniform — any page is electrically addressable |
| Overwrite | In place, directly | Never in place — erase-before-write, relocate-and-remap |
| Main scheduling goal | Minimize seek distance (SCAN, C-LOOK) | Maximize queue depth/parallelism across channels |
| Wear | None from writes | Bounded erase cycles per block — wear leveling required |
| Deletion signal needed | None — next write just overwrites | TRIM — otherwise the SSD preserves logically-dead data |

**How to decide:** treat these as genuinely different storage models, not "SSD = faster HDD." Code and OS defaults tuned for HDD assumptions (seek-minimizing schedulers, ignoring TRIM, assuming overwrite is cheap and free of side effects) can leave real SSD performance and lifespan on the table.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: DRAM vs SSD vs HDD latency, side by side
slides.markdown:
Rough, commonly-cited orders of magnitude worth memorizing for interviews: a DRAM access costs roughly 100 nanoseconds; a random 4KB read from a good NVMe SSD costs roughly 50-150 microseconds (500-1000x slower than DRAM); a random 4KB read from a 7200 RPM HDD costs roughly 5-10 milliseconds (another 50-100x slower than the SSD, and 50,000-100,000x slower than DRAM).

Sequential access narrows but doesn't erase this gap — sequential HDD throughput can reach 150-250MB/s, while a modern NVMe SSD sustains multiple GB/s sequentially. These numbers are exactly why "can the working set fit in RAM, and if not, is it at least on SSD rather than HDD" is one of the first questions in any real capacity-planning or performance-debugging conversation.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: over-provisioning as a lever the user doesn't see
slides.markdown:
SSD manufacturers reserve a chunk of raw flash capacity — often 7-28% depending on the drive class — that never appears in the drive's advertised usable capacity. This **over-provisioning** gives the garbage collector extra free blocks to work with at all times, directly reducing write amplification and improving sustained (not just burst) write performance, since the controller is less likely to be forced into servicing writes with no pre-erased blocks readily available.

A staff-level observation: users can manually increase effective over-provisioning by simply not using the drive's full advertised capacity (leaving 10-20% unpartitioned) — a real, practical technique for extending SSD lifespan and sustained write performance on write-heavy workloads (databases, heavily-logged systems), and a good example of understanding a hardware mechanism well enough to deliberately exploit it rather than just describing it.
